sections.h2: What makes selling a house in Clarksville, TN different?
sections.html:
Clarksville is the Montgomery County seat and sits about ten miles from Fort Campbell, where the 101st Airborne Division is stationed. The Census Bureau counts 22,758 veterans in the city for 2020 to 2024 and puts the July 1, 2025 estimate at 188,829 residents, up 13.2 percent from the 2020 base.

Homes are owned by 55.6 percent of households, the median owner-occupied value is $263,600, and median gross rent is $1,307. Only 9.6 percent of residents are 65 or older, against 17.3 percent in Chattanooga. A seller with permanent change of station orders may have a firm report date, and speed then outweighs squeezing out the last few thousand dollars.

A cash purchase on an as-is basis removes repair negotiation, showings and buyer financing from that clock. A conventional listing works when the house is move-in ready and the move date is flexible.

sections.h2: What does Clarksville look like on the map?
sections.html:
The city grew up where the Red River meets the Cumberland River, on the northwest edge of the Highland Rim about 45 miles from Nashville. It was founded in 1785, incorporated in 1807 and named for General George Rogers Clark. Austin Peay State University and the oldest newspaper in Tennessee, The Leaf-Chronicle, are based here.

The city covers 99.4 square miles of land and has 1,677 people per square mile, the densest of the four cities in this group. Main routes include U.S. 41A, which runs as Madison Street and Fort Campbell Boulevard, U.S. 79 along Wilma Rudolph Boulevard, Interstate 24 and State Route 76. Mean travel time to work is 27.0 minutes, the longest in this group.

Public schools belong to the Clarksville-Montgomery County School System, which operates 39 schools, including eight high schools. Portions of the city on Fort Campbell use the Department of Defense Education Activity. Employers named in the city's profile include Trane, Amazon, Google, LG, Hankook and Bridgestone.

sections.h2: Do Clarksville storms and floods change how a house sells?
sections.html:
They can, because the city has a recent record of damaging weather and buyers know it. A tornado ranked F3 hit downtown in January 1999, an EF2 struck the east side in February 2018, and the May 2010 floods damaged the city. In December 2023 an EF3 tornado crossed North Clarksville, killed four people and left more than 20,000 customers without power.

For a seller, the practical consequences are documentation and timing:

  • Keep roof, siding and window receipts, and note any insurance claim paid for storm damage.
  • Keep permits for repairs made after a storm, since a buyer's inspector will compare work to paperwork.
  • If the house was damaged and not fully repaired, describe the condition to buyers in writing and consider an as-is sale.
  • Check the flood risk for low lots near the Red River and Cumberland River before setting a price.

Cash buyers price the repairs they find, so an honest description up front speeds an offer.

sections.h2: How are Clarksville property taxes billed and paid?
sections.html:
The city and Montgomery County send separate bills. The City of Clarksville generates its bills from the file the county assessor sends, which lists whoever owned the property on January 1. Bills mail in October, taxes are payable from October 1 through the last day of February, and after that interest runs at 1.5 percent a month, or 18 percent a year, according to the city's property tax FAQ.

The city advises owners to check closing documents to see who is responsible for taxes, because a property can still go to a tax auction if taxes stay unpaid, whoever was supposed to pay. After a year of delinquency the city turns the account over to a delinquent tax attorney, and payments are then made at the Clerk and Master's office in Montgomery Chancery Court at 2 Millennium Plaza, Number 101.

Pay at Finance and Revenue, One Public Square, Suite 119, or at the North Center at 111 Cunningham Lane. Online payments carry a 2.5 percent processing fee. If a lender and an owner both pay, the city refunds the party that paid second. Call 931-645-7436 with questions. Ask Finance and Revenue at 931-645-7437 for the current city rate.

sections.h2: What tax relief can a Clarksville homeowner use?
sections.html:
The city lists two kinds of relief: one for elderly or disabled homeowners and one for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses. A first-time applicant signs up at the Montgomery County Trustee or at the City of Clarksville Finance and Revenue office, not both. The Trustee is at Veterans Plaza, 350 Pageant Lane, Suite 101-B, phone 931-648-5717.

Those approved for the age or disability category receive a voucher each year with the county and city bills and must bring income records to the city. Veteran-category recipients send signed vouchers to both the city and the county. The state pays the covered share only when the vouchers arrive.

The same Trustee office handles the Tax Freeze program, and the county notifies the city of an approved freeze. Ask the Trustee which documents each program requires before you apply.

sections.h2: Which Clarksville home rules can delay a sale?
sections.html:
City codes matter when a buyer's inspection turns up violations. The Codes Enforcement Division reviews property maintenance rules, takes complaints and offers a housing inspection request form. Its public FAQ says vehicles may not park on grass and must sit on concrete, asphalt or gravel. A fence taller than six feet needs a permit, and fences on a residential lot follow 30 or 40 foot front setbacks.

Pools get particular attention. Outdoor residential pools need a barrier at least 48 inches high, gates that close and latch themselves, and openings that stop a 4-inch sphere. Check an older pool and any fence near the setback line against these rules before a buyer's inspector does.

Call Building and Codes at 931-645-7426 to confirm a lot's zoning, and the Regional Planning Commission at 931-645-7448 about rezoning. Clear any open complaint before listing.

sections.h2: How is a Clarksville deed recorded and what does it cost?
sections.html:
The Montgomery County Register of Deeds is at 350 Pageant Lane, Suite 101-A, phone 931-648-5713, open 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. Its FAQ says the office cannot prepare documents or run title searches, requires original signed and notarized documents, asks for the preparer's name and address, and requires an oath of consideration on transfers unless a statute exempts the instrument.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Clarksville house quickly if I have PCS orders?
faqs.a: Yes, a cash sale can close on a date you choose, often within a couple of weeks if title is clear. Bring a payoff statement, the deed and any co-owner information. A written closing date lets you plan the move around your report date.

faqs.q: Who pays Clarksville property tax at closing?
faqs.a: The title company divides the year's tax between buyer and seller on the closing statement, based on the contract. The city bill goes to whoever owned the property on January 1. Review your closing documents so you know who sends payment, since unpaid taxes can lead to a tax auction.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Clarksville?
faqs.a: Record it with the Montgomery County Register of Deeds at 350 Pageant Lane, Suite 101-A. The phone number is 931-648-5713. Original signed and notarized documents are required, along with the oath of consideration on most transfers.

faqs.q: What does Tennessee charge on a Clarksville home sale?
faqs.a: The realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of price, which is about $975 on a $263,600 sale. A mortgage tax of $0.115 per $100 applies to secured debt above the first $2,000. Your title company shows both on the closing statement.

faqs.q: Is there property tax relief for Clarksville seniors?
faqs.a: Yes. The city and county offer relief for elderly and disabled homeowners and for disabled veterans, plus the Tax Freeze program. Apply at the Montgomery County Trustee, 931-648-5717, or at City Finance and Revenue, 931-645-7436, but not at both.
